source_user: A long-context workload intermittently hits OOM after several concurrent requests. Give a prioritized diagnosis and mitigations. Scenario variant 150: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: measure per-request KV growth and allocator fragmentation; check max sequence and batch; inspect active sequences; test paged/prefix cache, admission control, quantization, and context limits.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: GPU model and capacity, runtime/allocator versions, precision, parallelism, context limit, batching policy, cache implementation, and request-length/arrival distributions are unspecified; record them before interpreting an OOM. Treat intermittency as an observation, not proof of one cause. First preserve a crash-free baseline and the failing seed/arrival trace. For each request and device, timestamp admission, prefill, decode, eviction, and failure; record prompt and generated-token lengths, active sequences, batch membership, max-sequence settings, KV bytes/pages and bytes per token, allocated versus reserved memory, largest free block/fragmentation, weights, activations, workspaces, CUDA/NCCL allocations, and cache-page ownership. Check in order for a single request exceeding context/max-position limits, excessive concurrent long sequences or batch growth, anomalous KV growth, stale/leaked pages, allocator fragmentation, temporary workspace peaks, and replicated/topology-dependent allocations.

Falsifiable hypothesis: concurrent KV growth is exhausting the usable per-device headroom, with fragmentation amplifying the peak. Under a fixed replay, reducing the admission cap or maximum context should lower peak KV/reserved memory and eliminate OOMs without changing per-token KV slope; if it does not, inspect workspace, replication, or a leak. Run repeated randomized trials with the same model build, warmup, seed, arrival schedule, and request mix: baseline; conservative admission/context cap; paged KV/prefix caching; and, separately, lower-precision KV. Compare OOM rate, peak and P99 memory, KV bytes/token, fragmentation, TTFT/TPOT, throughput, queueing, and output correctness. Keep treatment only if correctness and SLOs remain acceptable with measured headroom.

Mitigate in increasing order of invasiveness: reject or queue requests using estimated KV demand and a reserved safety margin; cap context/concurrency and bound batch size; reclaim/expire pages safely; enable validated paged/prefix caching; tune allocator/workspace behavior; then consider KV quantization only after numerical and task-quality checks. Do not claim a fix from one run. Canary changes, monitor per-device memory and tail latency, and roll back on OOMs, corrupted or cross-request cache reuse, quality regressions, or SLO/headroom violations. Evidence required: synchronized raw traces, per-device telemetry, repeated control/treatment results, correctness checks, and rollback records.
risks: short or non-representative traces may miss the intermittent trigger
KV growth, fragmentation, workspace peaks, replicated weights, and cache leaks can be confounded
admission/context limits may reduce fairness, throughput, or tail latency
cache reuse or KV quantization may affect correctness, isolation, or model quality
evidence_required: raw synchronized request/token traces and exact replay inputs
per-device allocated/reserved memory, KV-page, allocator-fragmentation, workspace, and cache telemetry
repeated baseline/treatment trials with OOM rate, correctness, latency, throughput, and queueing results
canary and rollback records with explicit SLO and memory-headroom checks

Do not claim a fix from one run. Canary changes, monitor per-device memory and tail latency, and roll back on OOMs, corrupted or cross-request cache reuse, quality regressions, or SLO/headroom violations. Evidence required: synchronized raw traces, per-device telemetry, repeated control/treatment results, correctness checks, and rollback records.
